newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Guinness, GrandMet knock LVMH plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Guinness, GrandMet knock LVMH plan.

text.p: Britain's Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc knocked down rebel shareholder Bernard Arnault's LVMH demerger proposal on Friday, saying it would result in tax costs of 1.5 billion pounds ($2.5 billion).

French luxury goods and drinks company LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton was quick to hit back in what promises to be the most protracted and bitter Anglo-French tussle in corporate history, saying it would pursue its strategy of explaining its plan to investors.

The London market, now accustomed to the war of words between both sides, took the latest public duel in its stride. At 1135 GMT, GrandMet shares were down 6-1/2 pence at 612-1/2 while Guinness was down one at 597-1/2. LVMH shares in Paris were down eight francs at 1,604.

In a telephone conference call, GrandMet's chief executive John McGrath said the tax costs it would face if GMG Brands, the name given to Guinness and GrandMet's proposed merger, spun off fast food chain Burger King and food processor Pillsbury as proposed by Arnault in his rival plan would be too expensive for shareholders.
"Every investment bank has been at our door with proposals on how to get around that tax. Nobody has found a solution," McGrath said.
U.S. law forces a non-domicile business group to pay a one-off tax if it sells or spins off a subsidiary.

LVMH chairman Arnault, who has vigorously opposed the proposed 24 billion pound merger between Guinness and GrandMet since it was announced in May, is pressing for a demerger of Pillsbury, Burger King, and Guinness Brewing.

He also wants to create a separately quoted three way merger, DrinksCo, to include LVMH's drinks division Moet Hennessey, Guinness drinks arm United Distillers and GrandMet's IDV. Arnault's proposal lays claim to a 35 percent holding for LVMH shareholders in DrinksCo, although he has since shown flexibility in this demand.

The Breton entrepreneur claims that his plan would produce cost savings of 65 million pounds ($108.9 million) over and above the 175 million pounds already identified by the British companies two-way merger. But in a strongly worded rebuttal of Arnault's proposal, the two British companies dubbed the claims as "unrealistic".

In a joint statement George Bull, GrandMet chairman and Tony Greener chairman of Guinness said: "Under LVMH's proposals our shareholders would end up significantly worse off than under the GMG Brands proposal.
"An immediate demerger would destroy rather than create value and we cannot countenance LVMH taking value from our other shareholders in the manner proposed."
Both chairmen kept up a stony, unruffled tone in their statement despite constant pressure from Arnault's tactical manoeuvres in recent weeks.
"The GMG Brands merger is on track and the timetable is not affected by the arbitration," said both chairmen in the statement.
"Completion is targeted for January subject to regulatory and shareholder approval."
But they said they would still consider any future LVMH proposal that "adds to the value created by GMG Brands and which provides for a fair sharing of such incremental value."
They said the LVMH proposal was "fundamentally inequitable" and that LVMH's 66 percent share in drinks company Moet Hennessy was "not important to the success of GMG brands."
A spokesman for Arnault's camp said their statement added "nothing of value to the situation", and was "simply a padded assembly of their releases to date."
LVMH is the largest single shareholder in both British firms and has amassed an 11.06 percent stake in GrandMet by reducing his holding in Guinness to about 12.0 percent.

These shareholdings now enable him to convene an extraordinary meeting of shareholders in either group while giving him extra leverage at GrandMet, which needs a higher percentage of its shareholders to vote in favour of the merger than does Guinness.
Arnault, in London on Thursday, is expected to return here next week to visit more Guinness and GrandMet shareholders in an effort to win their support for his proposals.

Uncertainty over the outcome of the tussle has drawn the notice of credit rating company Standard & Poor's, which is considering putting the long-term senior debt rating for Guinness and GrandMet on CreditWatch with negative implications.
An S&P analyst told Reuters a final decision was likely later on Friday. He said there was now an added elemnt of uncertainity to the GMG merger plans.
($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
